statement: Scaling of maximal feeding rate with size should depend on transport network morphology.

scores.rationale: Several snippets bear directly on the claim that feeding/uptake scaling depends on transport network morphology. Snippets [1], [3], [7], and [14] explicitly discuss how anatomical resource-supply networks and transport models drive metabolic and assimilation scaling exponents (e.g., 3/4-power for network constraints vs 2/3 for surface laws), which directly links feeding/uptake rate scaling to transport morphology. Snippets [16] and [17] from Kooijman explain that feeding rates tend to be proportional to surface area when transportation costs scale with surface area, tying feeding scaling to transport/supply geometry. Snippets [4] and [15] show empirically variable exponents (often deviating from 2/3 or 2), consistent with the idea that morphology shapes the scaling rather than a single universal law. No snippet contradicts the fact; most relevant ones support it, though many remaining snippets merely describe DEB feeding formulations (surface-area-proportional uptake) without explicitly addressing network morphology. Support is moderate and coherent in direction, hence evidence_strength 2 and consensus_direction 3.

scores.rationale: The stylized fact concerns how the scaling of maximal feeding rate with body size depends on transport network morphology. Only a few snippets bear directly on this. Snippets [1] and [7] argue that a decelerating mean rate of water transport (a transport-network limitation) controls food uptake and maximum size in mytilid bivalves, offering partial support consistent with morphology/transport influencing feeding rate scaling. Snippets [2] and [9] discuss the West et al. fractal nutrient supply network model and Kozlowski's cell-size/number model, which link metabolic-rate scaling exponents to supply network geometry—conceptually supportive of the idea that transport morphology determines size scaling, though they address metabolic rather than feeding rate specifically. The remaining snippets concern social feeding, foraging behavior, offspring provisioning, and general life-history allometry, and are off-topic or only loosely related. No snippet contradicts the fact, but direct, quantitative evidence tying maximal feeding rate scaling to transport network morphology is sparse and indirect. Overall support is weak, with no conflict, leaving the evidence insufficient-to-mildly-corroborating.
